Agreed to provide pricing, security pack, and a small dedicated pilot proposal.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-12
Start time: 16:30 PT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Verdant Head of ML), Marco Ruiz (Verdant Platform), Sarah Boyd (Verdant Security), Tom (Verdant Product)
Shared artifacts: migration-playbook.xlsx (link shared), https://redwood.ai/docs/migration (doc), security_pack_v2.pdf (link)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for taking time today. Quick roll call — I see Lena, Marco, Sarah and Tom, is that everyone?
[00:05] Lena: Yep that's us, hi Alex.
[00:08] Marco: Hey.
[00:09] Sarah: Hi.
[00:11] Alex: Great. Priya and I will run through how we think about porting from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to the Redwood API, show the console/Optimize tooling for cost/perf, and then go into the parity mapping approach. We'll leave time for security questions.
[00:25] Priya: Quick agenda: 1) parity mapping strategy, 2) console walk — routing, model variants, rollouts, 3) Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization, 4) pilot plan and next steps.
[00:35] Tom: Sounds good. We're mainly focused on keeping latency under 250ms 95th for our chat endpoint and keeping cost per 1k tokens under a certain threshold.
[00:45] Alex: Perfect, that's helpful. If you can share your traffic shape later that's ideal. We're going to show how Redwood can match behaviors — streaming, role tokens, function call style outputs, and fallbacks to lighter quantized variants for cost savings.

[02:10] Priya: Alright, parity mapping. We start by mapping your current endpoints and their model families. Example: if you're calling gpt-4 style (OpenAI) and Claude v2 (Anthropic) — we map to Redwood catalog equivalents and pick profiles tuned for sequence lengths and cost. Important: we preserve prompt engineering patterns, stop sequences, and tokenization differences.
[02:40] Lena: Tokenization differences are big for us. We saw up to 8% delta when switching from Anthropic tokenizers to OpenAI tokenizer back in the POC. How do you handle that?
[02:52] Priya: We run a tokenization audit as step zero. Our migration-playbook.xlsx has a sheet where we run your prompt families across the candidate model tokenizers and surface deltas. Then we suggest small prompt rewrites or alternate model variants with closer tokenization behavior.
[03:10] Marco: Quick question on streaming — our UI depends on chunked streaming so users see partial responses — can Redwood match that?
[03:20] Alex: Yes. Streaming is supported in the Redwood API and the console shows stream traces. There's also a streaming fallback if you hit burst throttles. Note that streaming has a small memory/latency implication when using KV cache for long contexts.
[03:40] Sarah: (interject) Our security team will want to know about encryption in transit and KMS. Also audit logs for every token.
[03:48] Alex: Understood. We support TLS 1.2/1.3 in transit, at-rest encryption, and KMS integration. For Private deployments we can integrate with your HSM or cloud KMS. Audit logs include per-request metadata and token-level cost breakdowns. We'll send the security_pack_v2.pdf after the call.

[05:30] Priya: Moving to the console demo — I'm going to share my screen and show a sample migration that we've run for a similar customer. (screen sharing)
[05:50] Priya: Here is the model catalog. You'll see multiple Redwood-verified profiles: high-throughput, low-latency, quantized. For your chat flow we typically recommend starting with the low-latency profile and then plan a canary to a quantized variant for cost.
[06:20] Alex: We also have routing policies. You can route by latency SLO, cost cap, or region. So if an instance in us-west is overloaded we can fallback to a cheaper quantized instance in us-east and keep the endpoint up.
[06:38] Marco: How transparent is the fallback? Will the model signature change? That would break our downstream tool that expects structured assistant outputs.
[06:46] Priya: Good question. We keep model family compatibility and expose a schema compatibility check. If a fallback variant would yield incompatible outputs we can block the fallback or transform the output via a post-process lambda. The console shows compatibility warnings on rollouts.

[08:00] Priya: Now Optimize — this is our recommendations engine. We ingest your call logs (anonymized) and propose batching windows, cache TTLs, and quantization knobs tied to estimated cost savings and latency impact. For example, a 50ms batching window can reduce per-token cost by ~14% for your mix.
[08:30] Lena: Can Optimize account for 1:many prompt families where some prompts are latency-sensitive and others are throughput-only?
[08:40] Priya: Yes, you can tag routes. The optimizer will recommend per-route configs. You can also set hard SLOs per route and Optimize will avoid suggestions that violate SLOs.

[10:12] Marco: Let's talk about dedicated vs hosted. We want predictable throughput for peak business hours. Is dedicated the only option?
[10:20] Alex: Hosted can be fine if your traffic isn't spiky; it benefits from our multi-tenant pooling and often lowers cost. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable latency/throughput with SLAs. You can also do hybrid: dedicated with burst to hosted for extra traffic.
[10:42] Marco: What's the typical warmup time for a dedicated machine? We have strict cold-start constraints.
[10:50] Priya: Warmup depends on model size and KV cache priming. We recommend keeping a small hot pool warmed during business hours. The console has autoscale policies with min hot replicas to avoid cold starts.

[12:00] Sarah: Compliance: SOC2, ISO, SSO. We use SAML SSO and have audit forwarding to Splunk — can Redwood forward logs?
[12:10] Alex: Yes, Splunk, Datadog, CloudWatch — we stream audit logs. SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, RBAC scopes are supported. For Private deployments we can do a customer-managed control plane which helps with data residency.

[13:20] Lena: On the model side, we use Together for some specialized agents. Can Redwood run Together models or just map to equivalents?
[13:30] Priya: We primarily serve open models in our catalog, plus Redwood-verified builds. For Together-style models we either host the same model if licensing allows or map to the closest equivalent profile and tune via evals. We can also onboard a model binary for Private deployments if you bring the artifact under contract.

[15:00] Alex: Quick demo of the parity mapping sheet (opened). Column A is your endpoint name, column B upstream provider, column C current model, column D recommended Redwood model, column E expected token delta, column F suggested quantization, column G rollout plan.
[15:25] Tom: Nice. How do you estimate token delta? Is it deterministic?
[15:30] Priya: We run a small corpus of representative prompts through both tokenizers and report averages and worst cases. It's empirical not purely theoretical.

[17:05] Lena: We have about 30% of calls that use long context (12k tokens) — will we need KV cache management?
[17:13] Priya: Yes for that profile we recommend KV cache and prefix caching. It can reduce per-token compute by up to 60% for repeated context. There are tradeoffs for memory and eviction. The console exposes cache hit rate dashboards.

[19:40] Marco: Network egress: we have some regions that cannot reach public endpoints easily. How does Redwood handle VPC/private deployments?
[19:50] Alex: For VPC, the control plane can be customer-hosted and the inference plane sits in your VPC. We can do peering or private link and manage egress rules. For on-prem air-gapped, we have an offline package but that requires an enterprise license.

[22:00] Sarah: Can you describe the audit logs? We need per-request metadata with masked PII and integration to our SIEM.
[22:10] Priya: Audit logs include request id, route, model variant, latency, token counts, and SHA-256 hashes of prompts if you enable hashing for PII. We can set redact rules and forward to your SIEM. We'll include examples in the security pack.

[24:30] Alex: Let's walk through a hypothetical pilot. Step 1: parity mapping and tokenization audit. Step 2: small dedicated pool (2 GPUs) running your top chat route for 2 weeks with traffic mirroring. Step 3: evaluate latency/cost/responses and then canary a quantized variant.
[25:05] Lena: Mirroring is important to us. Do you support traffic mirroring live?
[25:12] Priya: Yes, we support synchronous mirroring with sampling and also async replay for non-prod. For production mirroring we recommend sampling to keep cost manageable.

[27:40] Marco: Any gotchas moving function-calling style prompts? We use structured JSON responses from the model.
[27:50] Priya: We support function/tool calling semantics similar to OpenAI's. We preserve name/type declarations and can validate JSON schema on return. If fallback variants yield non-conforming structs we block or auto-correct through schemas.

[30:00] Tom: Pricing — ballpark compare hosted vs dedicated for our mix (mostly chat, 2B tokens/month).
[30:10] Alex: High-level: hosted per-token tends to be higher unit price but you pay only for usage. Dedicated has fixed monthly commitment but lower per-token. We'll send a side-by-side with your volume and estimate potential savings from quantization and caching.
[30:40] Lena: We care about predictability for Q1.
[30:45] Alex: For that use-case we usually propose a reserved capacity with burst to hosted. We'll draft two SKUs in the proposal.

[33:05] Priya: Back to Optimize, here's an example recommendation. For one customer we suggested prioritized caching for the top 20 prompts, enabled 4-bit quantization on the low-latency fallback, and used a 30ms batching window for search endpoints. That saved ~38% cost while keeping p95 latency within their SLO.
[33:40] Lena: Do you have guardrails to ensure quality doesn't regress during quantization?
[33:48] Priya: Yes Optimize ties recommended changes to eval suites. We run an automated eval on your golden prompts and notify if quality falls below a threshold. You can also set automatic rollback.

[35:20] Marco: For the mirror pilot — what's the instrumentation we get? Traces, token breakdown, KV cache hit rate, per-request model variant?
[35:30] Alex: All of that and more. The console exposes route-level dashboards, trace waterfall, and a per-token cost breakdown. You can export logs to your data lake.

[37:00] Sarah: One more on KMS/HSM: we require that keys are separated by tenant and we rotate keys quarterly. Is that supported?
[37:10] Priya: Yes. Customer-managed keys, per-tenant key separation, rotation policies — supported. For Private deployments we can plug into your HSM for signing and key ops. We'll detail the architecture options in the security doc.

[39:00] Alex: Quick demo: canary rollout. (shows console) You pick traffic split, compatibility checks run automatically, and there's an automatic fallback policy if error rates or latency spike.
[39:25] Tom: Nice — can we schedule a dedicated SE-led benchmark next week to run our top-3 prompts under 95th p95 target?
[39:33] Priya: Absolutely. We recommend an isolated benchmark run on a dedicated pool to reproduce production-like concurrency and measure p95.

[41:10] Lena: For the migration spreadsheet — will you include recommended prompt rewrites or only model/quantization suggestions?
[41:18] Priya: We'll include both. For tokenization deltas we'll include suggested prompt edits, and for content differences we'll include evaluation notes and recommended threshold adjustments.

[43:00] Marco: Any limitations with Together models specifically? We use some Together proprietary stuff in a few agents.
[43:10] Alex: If a model is not redistributable we can't host it in our hosted catalog, but for Private deployments we can take the binary under a contract and run it in your VPC. Otherwise we map to a functional equivalent and run extra evals.

[45:05] Sarah: Ok last security ask — can we run a 3rd party pen test on the private deployment?
[45:12] Alex: Yes, with notice. For Private/on-prem we expect to coordinate and we have a pen test playbook. We'll add that to the security pack.

[47:00] Alex: Alright, recap and next steps. Priya will send the parity mapping template and example model profiles. I'll send pricing and the dedicated pilot SOW. Verdant to return prompt families and network constraints. We'll schedule the SE benchmark next week.
[47:25] Lena: Thanks folks, this was super helpful.
[47:30] Marco: Thanks.
[47:31] Sarah: Appreciate it.
[47:33] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with links.
[47:40] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-recognitions (e.g., "K V cache" for KV cache, "Samuel" for SAML), some speaker attribution sprinkled as "Tom" without role at times.
